title: Henry Ford and His Son Edsel
text:
Edsel Ford was the only child of Henry and Clara Ford. In 1919, at twenty-five, he became president of the Ford Motor Company. On paper he ran the firm; in practice his father kept control of every important decision.

Edsel had taste and a modern mind. He wanted Ford to offer more stylish cars, hydraulic brakes and new engines, as General Motors was doing with great success. Henry, who believed the Model T was all anyone needed, resisted for years while Ford lost market share. Edsel pushed through the purchase of the Lincoln company in 1922 and shaped the design of the Model A in 1927, but his father often overruled or humiliated him in front of others. Henry gave great power to Harry Bennett, the head of the company's security department, who undermined Edsel at every turn. Henry seemed to think his son was too soft and needed toughening.

Edsel worked under this strain for more than twenty years. He also became a generous supporter of the arts, funding Diego Rivera's murals at the Detroit Institute of Arts. In May 1943 he died of stomach cancer at forty-nine. Henry, nearly eighty, took back the presidency. Two years later, Edsel's widow Eleanor and Henry's wife Clara forced him to hand the company to Edsel's son, Henry Ford II.
lesson: A parent who cannot let go can crush the very successor he chose. Giving real responsibility means accepting decisions we would not have made.
people: Henry Ford, Edsel Ford, Clara Ford, Eleanor Ford, Harry Bennett
source: Douglas Brinkley, Wheels for the World (2003); Allan Nevins and Frank Hill, Ford (1954 to 1963)
